messages.author: c621ac38989fbf3c
messages.subject: speed question
parts:
I've taken on my most complex model to date, and it looks like it's going to take 4-5 full days to run on 4 cores with parallel processing.

the model is:

brm( result ~ s( long , lat , month ) + race*ethnicity + gender + age + ( 1 | ID ) , family="Bernoulli" , data=dat , future=TRUE , cores=4 )

My dataset is 36,000 data points, with result being a binary diagnostic testing variable with ~ 8000 positives

These 36,000 tests were done on 19,000 patients, so the ( 1 | ID ) term gives a random intercept to each of the 19,000 patients, controlling for repeat testing

race is a factor with 7 levels, ethnicity is a factor with 3 levels, the two are related and in a little glm race * ethnicity was superior to race + ethnicity

gender is a binary factor and age is a centered/scaled numeric


So with a 3-dimensional smooth, an interaction term, and a random intercept with 19,000 levels, this is taking FOREVER. I'm running this on a virtual machine with 16 GB RAM and 4 cores. It's taking around 24 hours per chain. Is this to be expected from a model of this complexity?

messages.author: 6e3dd74b422c061b
messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] speed question
parts:
Paul, since you seem surprised of the time it takes, I assume that all the other models were much faster(?)

The "problem" is likely the 3 dimensional spline, which could be too complicated for your data (depending on the distribution of the points in the 3D space). But we will only see this once the model is fitted.

You may try to replace s(...) by t2(...). Sometimes, this will consierably improve sampling speed.

Also, you don't want to use future=TRUE and cores > 1 at the same time. Essentially, when future =TRUE, cores will be ignored, since cores uses the built in parallel stuff of rstan, which is not called when future=TRUE (you will recieve a warning tell you this after having fitted the model).

So unless you want to use futures for some specific reason, just don't use the future argument at all and just go for cores = 4.

Best,
Paul

Hi Paul,

Well I'm not necessarily surprised - I've never run a model like this before and I expect it to be computationally intensive. Previous brms models I've run with a 2D smooth and more than 10,000 observations have taken much less time, though (8-10 hours for . 

Comparing the two smooths using mgcv s( ) looks better than t2( ) for these data:

> library(mgcv)
Loading required package: nlme
This is mgcv 1.8-19. For overview type 'help("mgcv-package")'.
> s_mod <- gam( result  ~ s( long , lat , month ) , family = "binomial" , data = dat )
> t2_mod <- gam( result ~ t2( long , lat , month ) , family = "binomial" , data = dat )
> anova( s_mod , t2_mod , test="Chisq" )
Analysis of Deviance Table

Model 1: result ~ s(long, lat, month)
Model 2: result ~ t2(long, lat, month)
  Resid. Df Resid. Dev      Df Deviance  Pr(>Chi)    
1     36614      34104                               
2     36660      34444 -45.904  -340.03 < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
